issues.legal_issue: Emergency powers cannot be used to dispense with the landowner hearing where the record does not establish a real and immediate urgency that would be frustrated by the time needed for an inquiry.
material_facts: The proposal to establish the sub-station had been under consideration for more than five years before the acquisition notification was issued.
More than a year passed after an official request cited the approaching power plant and major event as reasons for urgency before the preliminary notification was issued.
The Government produced no tangible evidence that the project had to be completed on a fixed schedule or that the time needed for objections and an inquiry would frustrate its purpose.
The approval dispensing with the hearing did not show a conscious assessment of why the hearing could not be held.

The project served a public purpose, but the asserted need to supply power and the project’s broad public benefit did not, without evidence of real urgency, establish that the hearing could be omitted.
issues.conclusion: The invocation of the emergency provisions and the resulting dispensation of the landowners’ hearing were unjustified; the acquisition was quashed, without preventing fresh acquisition proceedings in which the landowners could object and be heard.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5A(1) and 5A(2) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 protect the right to object and be heard. Sections 17(1) and 17(4) confer extraordinary powers that may be used to dispense with that inquiry only in a case of real urgency, where even the time required for the inquiry would probably frustrate the public purpose. The authority must apply its mind to relevant material, and its satisfaction is judicially reviewable. Pre-notification delay has material bearing on urgency, particularly where the Government produces no material justifying the elimination of the inquiry. A laudable public purpose or general public benefit alone does not justify denying a hearing. These principles are drawn from Anand Singh v. State of U.P. (2010) 11 SCC 242, Radhy Shyam v. State of U.P. (2011) 5 SCC 553, Munshi Singh v. Union of India (1973) 2 SCC 337 and State of Punjab v. Gurdial Singh (1980) 2 SCC 471; Deepak Pahwa v. Lt. Governor of Delhi (1984) 4 SCC 308 does not make pre-notification delay irrelevant in these circumstances. The Court also noted the protection against deprivation of property without authority of law under Article 300A of the Constitution.

predicates.emergency_land_acquisition_challenge: The proceeding challenges a compulsory land acquisition in which the acquiring authority invoked emergency powers and omitted the ordinary hearing of interested landowners.
predicates.extended_pre_notification_delay: The proposal for the acquisition remained under consideration for a substantial period before the preliminary acquisition notification was issued.
predicates.no_evidence_short_hearing_delay_would_fr: The acquiring authority produced no tangible evidence that the time needed for landowners to object and be heard would probably frustrate the public purpose.
predicates.no_conscious_assessment_of_need_to_omit_: The record did not show that the decision-maker consciously assessed why the landowners’ hearing had to be dispensed with.

issues.definition: When an emergency acquisition challenge involves substantial pre-notification delay, no evidence that the hearing period would frustrate the project, and no conscious assessment supporting omission of the hearing, the emergency dispensation is unjustified and the acquisition is invalid.
